entries.content: It's great that you're feeling better. Antidepressant adjustments involve many factors including how long you've been stable, the specific medication's half-life, and your individual response patterns. Your prescriber has access to your full history and can help you think through timing.

I've tapered three different SSRIs over the years and found that once you've successfully done a 50% reduction without issues, your body has basically shown it can handle that rate of change. My second and third tapers I just followed the same pattern that worked the first time. The initial successful taper is really your body telling you what pace works for you personally.

Reduced dose from 100mg to 50mg starting August 1st. Week 1-2: no noticeable withdrawal symptoms, sleep remained stable, mood consistent. The gradual approach from last time seems unnecessary in retrospect—body adjusted quickly to the halved dose. Worth remembering this tolerance pattern for future adjustments.

Discontinuation symptoms from SSRIs typically emerge within 2-4 days of dose reduction but can sometimes appear later. Symptoms may include dizziness, sensory disturbances, sleep disruption, and mood changes. The severity and timing vary considerably between individuals and between different reduction attempts in the same individual.

After my doctor helped me with my first taper and it went smoothly, I felt comfortable applying the same method on my own for subsequent adjustments. The first supervised taper taught me how my body responds—I learned I'm not particularly sensitive to dose changes. That knowledge has been valuable for making informed decisions about my own care without scheduling appointments for every small change.
